title: Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length
description: Brute force to optimized: recounting vowels from scratch for every window versus a fixed-size sliding window that adjusts a running count by one character at a time.

content.title: Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s and an integer k, find and return the maximum number of vowel letters in any substring of s having length exactly k. Vowel letters are a, e, i, o, and u.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The window length is FIXED at exactly k","A fixed-size sliding window"],["Every window shares almost all of its characters with its neighbor","Update a running vowel count incrementally instead of recounting the whole window"]]}

blocks.text: Given s and k, check every contiguous substring of exactly k characters, and return the highest count of vowels found in any of them.

blocks.title: Analogy: Scanning a Sentence Through a Fixed-Width Window
blocks.text: Picture sliding a small fixed-width window across a sentence, one letter at a time, and tracking the most vowels ever visible through that window at once.
The window "iii" contains 3 vowels, the maximum possible for any length-3 window here.
The best window, such as "eet" or "ode", contains 2 vowels.
Edge case: k equals the length of s
There is only one possible window, the entire string, so its vowel count is the answer directly.
Before recomputing every window's vowel count from scratch, notice that neighboring windows of a fixed size overlap almost entirely.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A window of length k moving forward by one position loses exactly its leftmost character and gains exactly one new rightmost character.

Observation 2: The new window's vowel count can therefore be derived from the previous window's count with one addition and one subtraction, not a full recount.

Observation 3: Count the first window's vowels directly, once, then slide forward, adjusting the count by whether the entering and leaving characters are vowels.

Observation 4: Track the maximum count seen across every window position.
This leads directly to a fixed-size sliding window that maintains a running vowel count instead of rescanning each window.
For every possible starting index, count the vowels in that length-k substring directly, and track the best count found.

items: For every starting index i from 0 to s.length minus k, examine the substring from i to i plus k minus 1.
Count how many of those k characters are vowels.
Track the maximum count seen across every starting index.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recount vowels from scratch for every window

codes.python:
def max_vowels(s, k):
    vowels = set('aeiou')
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(s) - k + 1):
        count = sum(1 for c in s[i:i + k] if c in vowels)   # recount every single window
        best = max(best, count)
    return best

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every window's vowel count is computed independently, with no memory of the previous window.
The inner loop re-examines all k characters for every one of the roughly n minus k plus 1 starting positions.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), recounting k characters for each of roughly n windows.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: almost all of that recounting work is repeated needlessly, since neighboring windows share all but one character.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recounting every window is wasteful: each new window differs from the previous one by exactly one character leaving and one entering.

What is the actual update needed: add 1 to the running count if the entering character is a vowel, subtract 1 if the leaving character was a vowel.

The core idea: count the first window once directly, then slide the window one step at a time, updating the count in O(1) per step instead of recounting.

Count the vowels in the first k characters directly. Then, for each position the window slides forward, add 1 if the newly entering character is a vowel, and subtract 1 if the character just leaving the window was a vowel, tracking the best count seen.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: add the entering character, drop the leaving one, track the best

blocks.text: Since each new window differs from the previous one by exactly one leaving and one entering character, adjusting the running count by those two characters alone always produces the exact vowel count for the new window, without ever re-examining the characters that stayed in the window.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass across the string.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: This is a textbook fixed-size sliding window: once the first window is counted, every later window is derived in O(1) by adjusting for exactly one entering and one leaving character.

items: Recomputing the vowel count from scratch for every window instead of adjusting incrementally.
Forgetting to check the leaving character, the one at index i minus k, not the one at index i minus k minus 1.

blocks.text: Explaining the window as "losing exactly one character and gaining exactly one" is the fastest way to justify why an O(1) per-step update is possible.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid recounting every window", think: count the first window once, then adjust by exactly the entering and leaving characters.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n times k) time; the optimized sliding window runs in O(n) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: fixed-size sliding window with an incrementally maintained count.
Core Idea: count the first window once, then adjust the running count by exactly the entering and leaving characters as the window slides.
Time: O(n times k) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized sliding window.
Most Important Observation: neighboring fixed-size windows differ by exactly one character on each side.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the fixed-window pattern is recognized.
One line memory trick: count once, then add the new, drop the old.
